To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the need for competence was related to both engagement and exhaustion.

the need for competence was a strong predictor of student engagement and exhaustion, students who endorsed mastery approach and performance avoidance goals, and who were more or less self-compassion and less or more physically active, reported greater engagement with and exhaustion from their medical studies, respectively, and students’ gender and year in medical studies predicted student engagement.

the need for competence, self-compassionate coping, and mastery approach goal orientations are important for engagement and that the need for relatedness, self-compassive coping, and mastery avoidance goals are important for exhaustion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how medical students cope with the challenges of medical education.
the relationship between the psychological needs and the coping strategies of medical students and their engagement and exhaustion in their studies.
the psychological and social determinants of burnout and engagement among medical students.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study found that the need for competence was a strong predictor of engagement and exhaustion in students.
the study findings support the need for a comprehensive and integrated student support and wellness program in medical schools.

the need for competence was found to be a significant predictor of student engagement and exhaustion, and students who endorsed mastery approach goal and who were more compassionate reported greater engagement with the medical school studies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the more students are able to meet their needs for autonomy, competence, relatedness, self-compassionate and mastery approach goals, and the more they are engaged in leisure-time exercise, the more engaged they will feel in their studies, and the more exhausted they will feel.

students who feel more competent, who engage in self-compassion and leisure-time exercise, who have mastery approach goals, and who have lower mastery avoidance goals will be more engaged and less exhausted from their medical studies.
the need for competence and self-compassion were the strongest predictors of student engagement and exhaustion, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that
medical schools should consider the psychological needs and coping strategies of their students to help them thrive during their medical education.
students who have a strong need for competence are more likely to be engaged with their studies and are also at greater risk of burnout-related exhaustion.
the need for competence, self-compassionate coping, and mastery approach goal orientation may help students cope with the demands of medical school and engage with their medical education.
